summary: This informational document describes principles of traffic engineering in the Internet, to improve understanding of the issues and give a common basis for developing capabilities. It covers architectures and methods for evaluating and optimizing operational networks. It first appeared as RFC 3272 in 2002, and this revision obsoletes that document.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic engineering is the work of deciding which path each flow of data should take through a network, so that no part of the network is overloaded while another sits idle. This memo gives the vocabulary for that work, the steps it takes, and the qualities a good traffic engineering system should have.

questions: what are the elements of traffic engineering
subtitle: The shared vocabulary and principles for steering traffic through IP networks so they stay fast, reliable and not overloaded.

tldr.problem: Operators need to measure and shape how traffic uses their networks, but traffic engineering spans many techniques and terms that had no common frame of reference.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terminology and a repeating process of policy, measurement, analysis and optimization, classifies TE systems on seven axes, surveys IETF techniques, and gives recommendations.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3272, a 2002 document, updating it with current practice and later IETF work. It is informational and sets no protocol rules.

facts.label: Performance measures
facts.value: Delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput

sections.title: What Internet Traffic Engineering Is
sections.content:
One of the most significant functions performed in the Internet is the routing and forwarding of traffic from ingress nodes to egress nodes, so the most distinctive function of Internet traffic engineering is the control and optimization of those functions, to steer traffic through the network. Internet traffic engineering is defined as that aspect of Internet network engineering dealing with the issues of performance evaluation and performance optimization of operational IP networks. It encompasses the application of technology and scientific principles to the measurement, characterization, modelling and control of Internet traffic.

It is the performance of the network as seen by end users that is paramount, and the characteristics visible to end users are the emergent properties of the network when it is viewed as a whole. A central goal of the service provider is therefore to enhance those emergent properties while taking economic considerations into account, by addressing traffic-oriented performance requirements while using network resources without excessive waste and in a reliable way. The traffic-oriented performance measures are delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput.

Internet traffic engineering responds to network events such as link or node failures, reported or predicted congestion, planned maintenance, service degradation and planned changes in the traffic matrix. Capacity management responds at intervals ranging from days to years, routing control functions operate at intervals ranging from milliseconds to days, and packet-level processing operates at a very fine temporal resolution. The optimization aspects can be viewed from a control perspective and can be both proactive and reactive: in the proactive case the control system takes preventive action against predicted unfavourable future network states, for example by engineering backup paths, and in the reactive case it responds to network events such as routing after a failure.

Another important objective of Internet traffic engineering is to facilitate reliable network operations, by providing mechanisms that enhance network integrity and by embracing policies that emphasize network survivability. The optimization aspects are achieved through capacity management and traffic management. Capacity management includes capacity planning, routing control and resource management, and the network resources of particular interest are link bandwidth, buffer space and computational resources. Traffic management includes nodal traffic control functions such as traffic conditioning, queue management and scheduling, and other functions that regulate the flow of traffic or arbitrate access to network resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic engineering is about choosing routes on purpose rather than by default. The goal is that the network as a whole behaves well for the people using it: low delay, little loss, and enough capacity to carry the traffic.

sections.title: The Three Elements of a TE Solution
sections.content:
The key elements required in any traffic engineering solution are policy, path steering and resource management. Some solutions rely on these elements to a lesser or greater extent, and debate remains about whether a solution can truly be called traffic engineering if it does not include all of them, but the document asserts that all TE solutions must include some aspects of all of these elements. Other solutions can be classed as partial TE and also fall within the scope of the document.

Policy allows for the selection of paths, including next hops, based on information beyond basic reachability. Early definitions of routing policy discuss routing policy being applied to restrict access to network resources at an aggregate level, and BGP is a commonly used mechanism for applying such policies. In the TE context, policy decisions are made within the control plane or by controllers in the management plane and govern the selection of paths. The definition of specific policies is left to the network operator.

Path steering is the ability to forward packets using more information than just knowledge of the next hop. Examples include IPv4 source routes, RSVP-TE explicit routes, Segment Routing and Service Function Chaining. Path steering can be supported through control plane protocols, by encoding information in the data plane headers, or by a combination of the two.

Resource management provides resource-aware control and forwarding, with examples of resources being bandwidth, buffers and queues, all of which can be managed to control loss and latency. Resource reservation is the control aspect of resource management: it provides domain-wide consensus about which network resources are used by a particular flow, and it may admit, reject or reclassify a flow based on policy. That consensus exists at the network control or controller level but not within the data plane. Resource allocation is the data plane aspect, providing the allocation of specific node and link resources to specific flows, including buffers, policing and rate-shaping mechanisms, and the matching of a flow to a particular set of allocated resources. Examples include Diffserv with dropping and remarking, MPLS-TE, GMPLS-based label switched paths and controller-based solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: Any traffic engineering system has three jobs. It states rules about which paths are allowed, it steers traffic along those paths, and it manages the capacity that the paths use. A system missing one of the three is only doing part of the job.

sections.title: The Process Model and the Taxonomy
sections.content:
The process model is a sequence of actions carried out to optimize the performance of an operational network, and it may be enacted explicitly or implicitly, by a software process or by a human. The model is iterative, and four phases are repeated as a continual sequence: define the relevant control policies that govern the operation of the network; acquire measurement data from the operational network; analyze the network state and characterize the traffic workload, where proactive analysis identifies potential problems that could manifest in the future and reactive analysis identifies existing problems and determines their causes; and optimize the performance of the network, which involves selecting and implementing a set of actions from a set of alternatives, using techniques that control the offered traffic and the distribution of traffic across the network.

Measurement is crucial to the TE function, because the operational state of a network can only be conclusively determined through measurement, and it is also critical to the optimization function because it provides the feedback data used to adaptively optimize network performance in response to events. Modeling, analysis and simulation are important aspects, because certain aspects of network performance studies can only be conducted effectively using simulation. Optimization can be corrective, with the goal of remedying a problem that has occurred or is incipient, or perfective, with the goal of improving performance even when no explicit problem exists.

The document then classifies traffic engineering systems along seven axes. On the first, systems are time-dependent, state-dependent or event-dependent: time-dependent methods use historical information about periodic variations to pre-program routing, state-dependent methods adapt plans to the current state of the network, and event-dependent methods are adaptive and distributed and typically search out capacity by learning models rather than by flooding available link bandwidth. On the second, systems are offline, meaning outside the network, or online, meaning within it. On the third they are centralized, distributed, or a hybrid of the two. On the fourth they use local or global information. On the fifth they are prescriptive, deciding what should happen, or descriptive, explaining what is happening. On the sixth they are open-loop or closed-loop. On the seventh they are tactical or strategic.
sections.plainLanguage: The work repeats: set the rules, measure what is happening, work out what it means, then act. The seven contrasts are the vocabulary an engineer uses to say what kind of system is being described.

sections.title: What a TE System Should Provide
sections.content:
The recommendations describe the capabilities needed to solve a traffic engineering problem or to achieve a traffic engineering objective. Functional recommendations describe the functions a traffic engineering system should perform, while non-functional recommendations relate to the quality attributes or state characteristics of such a system; these may contain conflicting assertions and may sometimes be difficult to quantify precisely. In a given context some recommendations may be critical while others may be optional, so prioritization may be required during development to tailor the system to a specific operational context.

The generic non-functional recommendations are these. Automation: whenever feasible, automate as many TE functions as possible to minimize human effort, which is particularly important in large-scale public networks because of the high cost of the human aspects of network operations and the high risk of network problems caused by human errors. Flexibility: allow for changes in optimization policy, with enough configuration options to tailor the system to a particular environment. Interoperability: develop systems and components with open standards-based interfaces. Scalability: remain functional as the network expands in routers, links, flows and traffic volume, without impairing other functions or consuming too many network resources. Security: safeguard the integrity of the TE system and protect the network from vulnerabilities that originate from breaches within it. Simplicity: keep the system as simple as possible, and hide complex algorithms and internal structures from the network administrator. Stability: stability refers to the resistance of the network to oscillate in a disruptive manner from one state to another, and state-dependent methodologies typically include a trade-off between responsiveness and stability, so it is strongly recommended that where such a trade-off is needed it be made in favour of stability, especially in public IP backbone networks. Usability: it should be easy to deploy in an existing network and easy to operate and maintain. Visibility: mechanisms should exist to collect statistics from the network and analyse them to determine how well the network is functioning.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks for systems that automate as much as they can, scale as the network grows, stay stable rather than flapping, and keep the operator's view simple. Where speed and stability conflict, it says choose stability.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering in Operational Networks
sections.content:
Service providers apply many of the TE mechanisms described in the document to optimize the performance of their IP networks, although others choose not to use any of them. The techniques include capacity planning, including adding equal-cost multipath options, for long timescales; routing control using IGP metrics and MPLS, as well as path planning and path control using MPLS and Segment Routing, for medium timescales; and traffic management mechanisms for short timescales.

Capacity planning is an important component of how a provider plans an effective IP network, taking into account the location of new links or nodes, equal-cost multipath algorithms, existing and predicted traffic patterns, costs, link capacity, topology, routing design and survivability. Performance optimization is usually an ongoing process in which traffic statistics, performance parameters and fault indicators are continually collected from the network; this empirical data is analysed and used to trigger TE mechanisms, and tools that perform what-if analysis can be used to review scenarios before a new set of configurations is implemented.

Real-time intra-domain TE using the IGP is done by increasing the OSPF or IS-IS metric of a congested link until enough traffic has been diverted away from it. Administrators of MPLS-TE networks specify link attributes and resource constraints such as maximum reservable bandwidth, a link-state IGP with TE extensions propagates topology and link attributes to all the routers in the domain, and the administrators specify the label switched paths that are to originate at each router, with attributes that indicate the requirements to be satisfied during path selection. RSVP-TE instantiates the paths, and by assigning proper bandwidth values to links and paths, congestion caused by uneven traffic distribution can be avoided or mitigated. If congestion occurs because of unexpected events, existing paths can be rerouted, or the reservable bandwidth of the congested links can be reduced to force some paths to be rerouted elsewhere.

Network management and planning systems have taken on much of the responsibility for determining traffic paths, which allows a network-wide view of resources and coordination of their use for all flows. Initial solutions using a path computation element to compute paths on behalf of routers have given way to an approach that follows the software-defined networking architecture. Segment Routing leverages a centralized controller and either an MPLS or IPv6 forwarding plane but does not need a signalling or management plane protocol to reserve resources in the routers, because all resource reservation is logical within the controller.
sections.plainLanguage: In practice, the everyday tools are the ones operators already have: raising a link's cost in the interior gateway protocol so traffic moves away, and reserving bandwidth on explicit paths with MPLS. The newer approaches move the decisions into a controller that computes paths for the whole network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In general, traffic engineering mechanisms are security neutral, and the document does not introduce new security issues. Network security is of course an important issue, and TE mechanisms can have benefits and drawbacks. TE may use tunnels that can slightly help protect traffic from inspection and that can in some cases be secured using encryption. TE puts traffic onto predictable paths within the network, which may make it easier to find and attack. TE often increases the complexity of operation and management of the network, which may lead to errors that compromise security. TE also enables traffic to be steered onto more secure links or more secure parts of the network, and can be used to steer traffic through network nodes that are able to provide additional security functions.

The consequences of attacks on the control and management protocols used to operate TE networks can be significant: traffic can be hijacked to pass through specific nodes that perform inspection or even be delivered to the wrong place; traffic can be steered onto paths that deliver quality below the desired quality; and networks can be congested or have resources on key links consumed. It is therefore important to use adequate protection mechanisms, such as authentication, on all protocols used to deliver traffic engineering.

Certain aspects of a network may be deduced from the details of the TE paths that are used. The link connectivity of the network and the quality and load on individual links may be inferred from knowing the paths of traffic and the requirements they place on the network, for example by seeing the control messages or through path-trace techniques. Such knowledge can be used to launch targeted attacks, such as taking down critical links, or can reveal commercially sensitive information, such as whether a network is close to capacity. Network operators may therefore choose techniques that mask or hide information from within the network. External control interfaces that provide additional control and management of TE systems give flexibility to management and to customers, but do so at the risk of exposing the internals of a network to potentially malicious actors, so the protocols used at these interfaces must be secured against snooping and modification, and use of the interfaces must be authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic engineering is not a security mechanism, and it can cut both ways: it can move traffic through an inspection point, and it can also reveal the shape of the network to somebody who wants to attack it. The rules that steer traffic are therefore as worth protecting as the paths they protect.

messages.label: DEFINE POLICY
messages.note: Set the rules that govern how the network is to be used.

messages.label: MEASUREMENT DATA
messages.note: Collect data from the operational network.

messages.label: ANALYZE
messages.note: Proactive analysis finds problems that could appear; reactive analysis finds existing ones.

messages.label: OPTIMIZE
messages.note: Choose and implement actions that control the offered traffic and its distribution.

viz.caption: THE QUALITIES A TE SYSTEM SHOULD HAVE

items.title: Automation
items.text: Automate as many TE functions as possible, because human effort is expensive and human error is risky.

items.title: Flexibility
items.text: Allow the optimization policy to change, with enough configuration options to suit the environment.

items.title: Interoperability
items.text: Use open standards-based interfaces so that systems and components can work together.

items.title: Scalability
items.text: Keep working as routers, links, flows and traffic volume grow, without hogging network resources.

items.title: Simplicity
items.text: Keep the system simple, and hide complex algorithms and internal structures from the administrator.

items.title: Stability
items.text: Resist flapping between states. Where responsiveness and stability conflict, choose stability.

items.title: Usability
items.text: Easy to deploy in an existing network and easy to operate and maintain.

items.title: Visibility
items.text: Collect statistics and analyse them, so that the state of the network can be judged.
